catalog_quote: In this study, the term 'tone' is used to classify the pitch on individual syllables. The pitches are arranged in certain patterns termed 'tone patterns'. The term 'intonation' is used for modifications of an entire tone pattern, e.g., raising the general pitch level while the relation of the individual tones to each other remains constant. ... There are three phonetic ranges of pitch, and there are restrictions on the distribution of the top and middle ranges. ... The system is analysed as having two contrasting tonemes, low tone and high tone, plus a feature of upstep which gives rise to the top pitch. The upstep feature is of two types: automatic upstep and the upstep toneme which are described below. tone_statements.citation: Snider, Keith (1998/9). Tonal ‘upstep’ in Engenni. Journal of West African Languages 27. pp. 3-15.
tone_statements.quote: Although Thomas (1974, 1978) describes Engenni, a Kwa language spoken in Nigeria, as having three levels of surface pitch with restrictions on the top and middle levels, she analyzes the system as having only two contrasting tonemes, low and high. In addition there is what she calls “automatic upstep.” ... Upstep in Engenni is predictable and results in the shifting upwards of a high tone whenever a low tone follows the high.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, section 1 'Engenni'; same statement in the abstract, p. 3
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones (low, high), three surface pitch levels; Thomas's 'automatic upstep' of H before L reanalysed (Register Tier Theory) as incomplete downstep: highs downstepped after a lexical, floating or boundary low; the 'superhigh' is a non-downstepped H. Data from Thomas; nothing on stress.

(2) Deciding source: Thomas 1978 is the standard and only reference grammar of Engenni (published SOAS 1969 thesis); Glottolog lists no later grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study, and the later tone literature (Thomas 1974, Snider 1999 JWAL, Hyman 2000) is built entirely on Thomas's data and uniformly treats Engenni as a two-tone (H/L) language with upstep/three surface levels; none mentions stress or accent. sources.quote: Engenni, a Kwa language spoken in Nigeria, has three levels of surface pitch with restrictions on the top and middle levels. There are only two contrasting tones: low and high. In addition there is what Thomas (1978) calls "automatic upstep." The upstep is predictable and results in the upstep of a high tone whenever a low tone follows the high. [...] In Engenni, as in many West African languages, a high tone that follows a low tone is always lower than a high tone that precedes the low tone, but higher than the low tone itself. This is typically called downdrift or automatic downstep [...] So I conclude that the superhigh tone in Engenni is simply a non-downstepped high.
sources.note: Confirms the catalog's lexical-tone coding (two contrasting tones, low and high; Thomas 1978 is the catalog's cited source and Snider's sole data source) and adds surface-register detail: three surface pitch levels; downdrift/automatic downstep (H after L lower than H before L); Thomas's 'automatic upstep' of a H immediately before a L (also when the L's vowel is elided) reanalyzed as a non-downstepped high under Register Tier Theory, with a floating l register boundary tone at the left edge of phonological phrases lowering initial highs. No lexical tone inventory beyond H/L; no word-stress, s

Engenni as downstep cases).
